clue.text: Offence clearly announced in court

definitions.meaning: a misdeed or wrongdoing, something one is to blame for
on a tennis court the umpire calls out loud when a serve lands outside the service box

explanation.surface: A crime is read out plainly before the judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court, which suits 'Offence', but the second sense is a tennis court, where a bad serve is called.
explanation.definitionFit: A misdemeanour is a lapse one is blamed for, and a tennis umpire calls the same word for a serve that misses the box.

clue.text: King's soon trapped by this jester's wife

definitions.meaning: the quickest checkmate in chess, delivered on the second move
the spouse of a court clown

explanation.surface: A monarch is quickly caught out by his clown's spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess sense needs knowing that the shortest possible checkmate has this name; read literally, it is the partner of a court jester.
explanation.definitionFit: The two-move checkmate is named as if it were the spouse of a jester, since a jester is a professional idiot and a spouse is a partner.

clue.text: Incompetent figurehead in fighting group

indicators.note: the head letter is placed inside the military group

parts.note: a unit is a body of soldiers
the head of the word figure is its first letter, F

explanation.surface: A useless leader sits at the top of a military band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figurehead' looks like a nominal leader, but it gives the head (first letter) of 'figure', which goes 'in' UNIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not up to a task is lacking the competence or fitness needed for it.

clue.text: First-class fare for Empress of Blandings required on vessel

parts.note: top means best, first-rate
the Empress of Blandings is the prize pig in P. G. Wodehouse's Blandings stories, and mast is nuts fed to pigs

explanation.surface: Premium food for a famous pig is needed aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The Empress of Blandings is Lord Emsworth's champion sow in P. G. Wodehouse's comic novels; mast is the beech and oak nuts pigs eat.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper section of a ship's mast is a spar a sailing vessel needs to carry its upper sails.

clue.text: Cold War missiles?

parts.note: read literally, these are weapons in a war fought with cold things, packed handfuls of frozen flakes thrown in winter play

explanation.surface: A question about the weapons of the US-Soviet stand-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold War' points to the US-Soviet rivalry and its rockets, but here it is a winter fight where the missiles are made of frozen flakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Packed balls of frozen flakes are the projectiles of a winter fight, a war that is literally cold.

clue.text: It might be a familiar drink

definitions.meaning: a familiar is a witch's attendant demon, a supernatural being
strong liquor such as whisky or gin

explanation.surface: Something that could be a regular tipple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Familiar drink' reads as a usual tipple, but 'familiar' is the noun for a witch's attendant ghost.
explanation.definitionFit: A witch's familiar is a supernatural being or ghost, and distilled liquor such as gin is also known by the same word.

clue.text: Trio sang composition for another musician

indicators.note: a composition arranges parts into a new order, so these letters are put together afresh

explanation.surface: Three singers perform a piece written for one more player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composition' looks like the music the trio sings, but it is the signal to rearrange TRIOSANG.
explanation.definitionFit: A keyboard player in a church plays the pipe instrument, so is one more kind of performer of music.

clue.text: Obstruct love, making no exceptions

parts.note: to bar is to block or obstruct
love is a zero score in tennis, so nothing at all

explanation.surface: Forbid romance entirely, with no allowances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' as nil in tennis scoring stands for nothing, written out as the word for not any.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning without exception, excluding nobody from the statement.

clue.text: Landlord has separate compartment for his correspondence

parts.note: a letter is one who lets property to tenants
to box something off is to separate it into a compartment

explanation.surface: A property owner has his own private pigeonhole for his mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Landlord' gives one who lets, a letter; the word then doubles as mail, which suits the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A slot or receptacle where post is delivered holds the mail sent to a household.

clue.text: In cunning way, dramatist put second first

indicators.note: the abbreviation for second is placed before the playwright's name

parts.note: John Lyly was an Elizabethan playwright

explanation.surface: A playwright reorders his work, putting the second scene first.
explanation.walkthrough: John Lyly was an Elizabethan playwright and author of Euphues; 'put ... first' places S (second) ahead of his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting craftily or with guile is behaving in a sly fashion.

clue.text: Children like a broken jack-in-the-box, possibly

definitions.meaning: a toy whose coil has come away has its spring off

explanation.surface: Kids resemble a toy that no longer pops up.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words: a broken jack-in-the-box may have its coil detached, its spring off.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's descendants or young are the issue that springs from them.

clue.text: Hear again about sporting achievement

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a try is a score in rugby

explanation.surface: Listen once more to news of a feat on the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear' is meant in the legal sense of a court hearing a case; a TRY is a touchdown score in rugby.
explanation.definitionFit: A court that hears a case a second time puts it on trial again.

clue.text: Programme — some miss it completely when it's cut

parts.words: some miss it completely when it's cut
parts.note: some of the letters of miss it completely spell the clipped name of this genre of television show, which is what it becomes when shortened

explanation.surface: Some people skip a television show entirely when it is edited down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' hides SITCOM in 'misS IT COMpletely', and SITCOM is what the answer becomes 'when it's cut' to an abbreviation; the full form has to be supplied.
explanation.definitionFit: A comic broadcast series built around recurring characters in one setting is a type of television show.

clue.text: Keenness to get vacuum without lead

indicators.note: the leading letter of the word for emptiness is dropped

parts.note: vacuity is emptiness, a vacuum

explanation.surface: Being sharp enough to obtain a vacuum cleaner without a cord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without lead' suggests a flex, but it removes the first letter of VACUITY, the V.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharpness of mind or sight is keenness of perception.

clue.text: Superior example — capital sort of 7

parts.note: upper means higher or superior
a case is an instance or example

explanation.surface: A fine specimen of a great kind of postbox.
explanation.walkthrough: 7 is LETTERBOX, so the cross-reference stands for its first part: capital letters are the large ones, named after the printer's upper type tray.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital letters are the large forms of the alphabet, from the higher tray a typesetter kept them in.

clue.text: Bless me specially after a mass

indicators.note: the rearranged words come after the single letter A
the words are rearranged in a special way, signalling a new order

explanation.surface: A priest's blessing given after a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' looks like the church service, but it is a verb, to gather; 'specially' rearranges BLESSME into SSEMBLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To mass troops is to gather or bring them together in one place.

clue.text: Fearless when beheaded, all right

indicators.note: the first letter of the compound meaning unafraid is removed

parts.note: terror-free means without fear

explanation.surface: Bold even after execution, and quite fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When beheaded' drops the first letter, T, from TERROR-FREE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without a single mistake is correct, faultless and so in order.

clue.text: Inherit unnamed trio of these

parts.note: the word inherit splits into in, her and it, and words like her and it stand in for a noun so that the thing need not be named

explanation.surface: A command to receive a legacy of three anonymous items.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inherit' splits as IN-HER-IT; HER and IT, and I and HE inside, are words used in place of a name, which is why they are 'unnamed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Words such as she, it and they substitute for nouns, standing in for an unnamed person or thing.

clue.text: Vote in Europe's oddly revealing

indicators.note: the voting mark goes inside the rearranged letters
oddly here means strangely, signalling the letters of the word are jumbled

parts.note: X is the mark made on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: A ballot in Europe is strangely telling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like a pick of alternate letters, but here it rearranges EUROPES, with X (a vote) placed 'in' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Laying something bare is uncovering it, the act of making it visible.

clue.text: Do record half-century in 21, perhaps

indicators.note: the Roman fifty goes inside the rearranged almanac name
perhaps suggests the letters of the cross-referenced answer might be in some other order

parts.note: the answer to 21 down, the cricket almanack
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Score a record fifty in the cricket almanack, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' is the verb to cheat; 'perhaps' rearranges the 21-down answer and L (fifty) goes 'in'; 'record' is a link reading as enter.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone is slang for cheating or defrauding them.

clue.text: Not a full house — needs a ten, king or joker

indicators.note: the shortened dwelling needs the next letters inside it
the house is not complete, missing two of its letters

parts.note: taken as written
X is the Roman numeral ten
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A poker hand short of a full house wants a ten, a king or the wild card.
explanation.walkthrough: The poker scene misleads; HOUSE loses US to give HOE, which 'needs' A and X (ten) inside, then R (rex) for king.
explanation.definitionFit: A prankster who plays tricks to fool people is a practical joker.

clue.text: Moronic error in Aristotle's spelling

indicators.note: an error puts the letters in the wrong order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A foolish mistake in the way Aristotle spelt words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Aristotle's spelling' is the definition: a letter of the Greek alphabet, which Aristotle wrote in.
explanation.definitionFit: The short O of the Greek alphabet is a letter Aristotle would have used when writing.

clue.text: Cricket authority's to stretch a point internally

indicators.note: the compass point is placed inside the verb for broadening

parts.note: to widen is to stretch or broaden
S, south, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A cricket umpire's job is to extend a rule a little.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the annual cricketers' almanack, long regarded as the game's book of record.
explanation.definitionFit: The yearly cricketers' almanack is the standard reference book on the sport.

clue.text: Monsieur, perhaps, holds in statesman

indicators.note: the phrase for a Frenchman's title contains the next word

parts.note: monsieur is the French form of mister, so a mister from abroad

explanation.surface: A Frenchman keeps a politician indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monsieur, perhaps' is a FOREIGN MISTER, the 'perhaps' flagging an example; it 'holds' IN after its M.
explanation.definitionFit: A government member running a nation's dealings abroad is a senior politician.

clue.text: After four, this game produces score

definitions.text: After four, this game produces score

parts.words: After four, this game produces score
parts.note: the plural of the number after four names a handball court game, and four of that number multiply to a score, twenty

explanation.surface: A sport played after four o'clock yields a result.
explanation.walkthrough: The number after four is five; four fives make twenty, a score; and the plural is also a handball-type court game played at English schools.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural of the number after four names a court game played by striking a ball with the gloved hand.

clue.text: Characters preceding US foe, in a fashion

parts.note: each letter of us and foe is replaced by the letter just before it in the alphabet

explanation.surface: Letters written ahead of an American enemy, styled in a certain way.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letter before each of U, S, F, O, E in the alphabet: T, R, E, N, D.
explanation.definitionFit: A prevailing style or vogue is the current fashion.

clue.text: Beginnings of virtue as well as delicacy

parts.note: the opening two letters of the word virtue
and means also, as well as

explanation.surface: The roots of goodness and of refinement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delicacy' looks like refinement of manner, but it is a choice food; 'Beginnings' takes two letters here, not one.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for an item of food, especially a choice dainty dish.

clue.text: Bravest when divided, for example

parts.note: split the word bravest into bra and vest, two garments worn beneath clothes

explanation.surface: The most courageous, once split up, as an illustration.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'Bravest' into BRA and VEST: both are examples of garments worn beneath outer clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Bras and vests are items of clothing worn beneath outer garments, next to the skin.

clue.text: Rocket designer, say, and American statesman

indicators.note: say signals a word spoken, so the engineer's surname is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: George Stephenson built the early steam locomotive called Rocket

explanation.surface: An engineer of rockets, perhaps, and a US politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocket' suggests space travel, but it is the 1829 steam locomotive; Adlai Stevenson was a US presidential candidate and UN ambassador.
explanation.definitionFit: Adlai Stevenson was a Democratic presidential nominee and US ambassador to the United Nations.

clue.text: Gently push, for instance, horse that's backed

indicators.note: backed means read from end to start, turning the whole run of letters round

parts.note: eg is short for exempli gratia, for example
a dun is a greyish-brown horse

explanation.surface: Lightly prod, say, a horse that has been bet on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' suggests a betting horse, but it reverses EG plus DUN.
explanation.definitionFit: To prod someone lightly with the elbow is a gentle push to draw attention.
